ID-2026-H516.s: This law changes Idaho school labor rules and bars school districts from using taxpayer money to support teachers unions in set ways, such as dues deductions, certain payments, or paid leave for union work unless the law allows it. It also sets rules for negotiations between school districts and teacher groups, defines terms like teacher union activities, and adds civil penalties for violations. It took effect on July 1, 2026, and applies to certain contracts made or changed on or after that date.

ID-2026-H542.s: Idaho’s law creates rules for large social media platforms that have at least $1 billion in ad revenue worldwide in one of the past three years. It says these platforms must estimate a user’s age after certain use levels, require a birth date when someone signs up, and get verifiable parental consent before making or keeping an account for a child under 16 or changing that child’s account settings. For child accounts, privacy settings must start at the most private level, and the law took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H621.s: The bill would change Idaho’s rules on where people with concealed weapon permits, or those carrying under the law, may not carry a concealed weapon. It would also define "courtroom portions of a courthouse" to include the courtroom, judges' chambers, witness rooms, jury rooms, attorney conference rooms, prisoner holding cells, and some nearby offices and hallways. It would make technical changes and take effect on July 1, 2027.

ID-2026-H721.s: The law changes how public school building plans are reviewed in Idaho. A school district may choose either the state division or a local government to review plans, and the review must be done within 30 days. It also says which kinds of workers can do these reviews, sets fee limits, and takes effect July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H730.s: Idaho changed its SNAP rules to add more checks on eligibility and to review more state and federal records for changes that could affect benefits. It also requires the state to share some public, nonprivate data about SNAP fraud and improper payments on its website. The law took effect on July 1, 2026, and applies to people who get or apply for SNAP benefits.

ID-2026-H758.s: The bill would change Idaho daycare rules on watching children while they sleep and on how some children are counted for staffing limits. It would allow live video and audio monitoring for a sleeping child if the provider stays close enough to help right away. It would also say a provider’s own children age 5 or older do not count in the attendance total for a family daycare home or group daycare facility when the provider works out of their home. It would take effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H810.s: The law changes the rules for people who want to run for state representative or senator in Idaho. They must live in the district for one year before filing and must have actually stayed there at least 120 nights during that year. People on active military duty get an exemption from the 120-night rule. It takes effect on January 1, 2027.

ID-2026-H817.s: Idaho law now updates rules for selling cigars and other tobacco products. It adds terms for things like cigar-related products, mobile cigar retailers, and designated cigar gardens, which are outdoor areas at events for people 21 and older. It also changes permit rules, sales methods, and sample rules for tobacco products and electronic smoking devices. The law takes effect July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H822.s: The law creates rules for schools, child care providers, and health or mental health providers about a minor child’s sex transition or social transition. It says these covered groups must inform parents, get written parent consent before helping with a social transition, and may not help with sex transition procedures. It also lets parents sue, gives the attorney general power to investigate and seek penalties of up to $100,000, and takes effect July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H883.s: Now law, this measure creates an earned-autonomy program for school districts and public charter schools that meet set test scores, graduation, and audit standards. Eligible schools can spend certain state funds with more freedom and may be excused from some reporting rules without losing funding. The state board of education must report in 2029 on how many schools take part and any changes in student growth or test scores. It takes effect July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H887.s: The law changes Idaho rules for towing water skiers and adds cases where the boat does not need a second person as an observer. It allows that exception when the boat has a firm rearview mirror that lets the driver see the skier, and in some slalom course and certain time-of-day situations. The law took effect on April 2, 2026.

ID-2026-H896.s: The bill would set up a process for the attorney general to handle claims that a public officer, public employee, or public agency broke certain Idaho laws. It would require notice and a chance to fix the issue first, then allow a court order to make them comply if needed. In some cases, it would also allow removal from public office or public employment for up to five years and let the winning side recover attorney fees.

ID-2026-H897.s: The bill would change Idaho tax breaks for data centers and some large new business investments. For data centers started on or after April 1, 2026, the sales tax break would apply only to eligible server equipment, and businesses would also have to meet set job, power, and water notice rules to keep the break. It would also limit a property tax break for new capital investments to projects that began construction before April 1, 2026, which would affect businesses, counties, and local taxing districts.

ID-2026-H928.s: This law adds a new section to Idaho law called the Merit-Based Health Care Act. It sets rules for Medicaid-funded health care providers on hiring, training, and public messages, and it bars certain diversity, equity, and inclusion practices in those settings. The attorney general may investigate complaints and seek civil penalties, and health care workers may sue for retaliation in limited cases. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H929.s: The law lets people with health coverage pay a lower cash price for covered care and have that amount count toward their deductible and yearly out-of-pocket limit if they send the needed proof to the insurer. Providers must accept that cash payment as payment in full and cannot bill the rest to the person or the insurer. It does not change prior approval, medical need rules, or use rules in the health plan, and it takes effect on January 1, 2027.

ID-2026-H930.s: Idaho would change the rules for political treasurers, who handle campaign money for candidates and political committees. It would make the treasurer the main contact for the secretary of state and keep the current rules for tracking money, filing reports, and keeping campaign funds separate. The law took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H931.s: The law changes the Portable Benefit Plan Act by removing one definition from the state code tied to the plan. It affects the rules for portable benefit accounts and portable benefit plans used by independent contractors, and it involves banks, insurance, and other plan providers. It takes effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H932.s: The law asks Idaho voters in the 2026 general election to pick a gun to be named the state gun. It directs the Secretary of State to put the question on the ballot and count the results, and the Legislative Council may add more gun choices before the final list is filed. The law took effect on April 2, 2026.

ID-2026-H934.s: The bill updates Idaho’s parental choice tax credit, a refundable tax credit for certain K-12 education costs, and it became law with retroactive effect to January 1, 2026. It sets the credit at up to $5,000 per eligible student, or up to $7,500 for eligible students with disabilities, and allows some parents to get an advance payment. It also adds rules for who can claim the credit, a $50 million yearly cap, and reporting and survey requirements.

ID-2026-H959.s: Idaho law now lets fire protection districts and ambulance service districts use an initiative petition to raise or lower their property tax budgets. It sets the steps for those petitions, including who may sign, how many signatures are needed, and when the vote would happen. The law also changes property tax budget limits for these districts, including a higher cap on budget growth, and it applies retroactively for some parts and on July 1, 2026 for others.

ID-2026-H964.s: Idaho’s Department of Fish and Game will get $14,178,500 for fiscal year 2027. The money is for administration, fisheries, and wildlife work, and some unused dedicated and federal funds from fiscal year 2026 can be used again for nonrecurring costs. Also, $200,000 from the Fish and Game Other Fund must be used to improve wolf trapping to manage wolf predation, and the law takes effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H965.s: The law changes funding for the Office of Species, Minerals, and Energy Coordination and the Idaho State Historical Society for fiscal year 2027. It gives the office $1,699,700 and adds 12 full-time positions, while reducing the historical society’s appropriation by the same amount and cutting 12 positions. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H972.s: It provides extra money to the Department of Health and Welfare’s Division of Welfare for administration of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program in fiscal year 2027. The bill sets aside $351,000 from the General Fund and $163,000 from a federal fund, for a total of $514,000. It became law as Chapter 332 and took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H973.s: The law gives the Military Division an extra $6.5 million from the Federal Grant Fund for fiscal year 2026. The money is for operating costs to replace climate control systems in Air National Guard buildings at Gowen Field. It took effect when it was passed and approved.

ID-2026-H974.s: The bill gives additional money to the Idaho State Police for fiscal year 2027. The funds are for personnel costs in the director’s office, capitol protective services, investigations, patrol, and law enforcement programs. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-H976.s: The law directs the state controller to transfer money from interest earnings to two funds: 60% to the Strategic Initiatives Program Fund and 40% to the Local Highway Distribution Fund. The transfer is 50% of certain interest earnings from fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026, or $32,877,300, whichever is greater. It took effect on April 10, 2026.

ID-2026-H978.s: The bill sets the 2027 budget for Idaho’s Department of Health and Welfare public health services division. It gives money for immunization, lab services, and suicide prevention, while also cutting some funds and reducing three full-time jobs. It also requires several reports by December 31, 2026, and took effect on July 1, 2026, except for the governor’s line-item veto in Section 3.

ID-2026-HCR29.s: A House concurrent resolution is a formal statement by lawmakers. It says the Idaho Legislature finds the Muslim Brotherhood and the Council on American-Islamic Relations to be foreign terrorist organizations and says it will treat them that way in future legislation. It also says this could matter for future bills about buying or acquiring land in Idaho.

ID-2026-S1247.s: The bill would require covered employers in Idaho, including public agencies and some large private employers that do business with public agencies, to use the federal E-Verify system to check new hires. It would make it unlawful for those employers to knowingly hire or refer a worker whose work status has not been checked, and it sets steps for state enforcement and court penalties. The law would take effect on January 1, 2027.

ID-2026-S1313.s: The law lets pharmacists who meet the listed training and testing rules choose to get a naturopathic doctor license in Idaho. It also updates the rules for the naturopathic board’s formu lary committee, which advises on prescription issues, and says one committee member must be a licensed pharmacist who is not licensed under this chapter. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1330.s: The law raises the small claims limit for money claims and personal property claims from $5,000 to $15,000. It also keeps a $25 attorney fee for a winning party after an appeal and adds a $20 appeal fee paid to the county treasurer for the court technology fund. It takes effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1336.s: The law changes Idaho school rules for civics and history teaching. It adds more required lessons on the U.S. Constitution, American founding documents, Idaho history, and how government works for public school students, especially in secondary school. It also keeps rules for flag display, the pledge or national anthem, and the civics test, and it took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1351.s: The bill would bar a governor from reappointing a person to the same state job for one year after the Senate has expressly rejected that person. It would also require the governor to fill certain Senate-confirmed appointments and vacancies within 90 days, or by the start of the next legislative session if sooner. The act would take effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1356.s: This law changes how commissioners are chosen in certain single countywide highway districts. It adds primary elections starting with the 2028 elections and updates filing and write-in rules for those district races. It also makes related ballot and election law changes for these district offices.

ID-2026-S1359.s: The bill would create rules for virtual currency kiosks in Idaho. It would require kiosk operators to be licensed money transmitters and to follow reporting, disclosure, customer service, receipt, and fraud prevention rules. It would also set limits for new customers, require refunds in some fraud cases, and was later vetoed.

ID-2026-S1429.s: This law changes funding for Idaho’s Health and Welfare Department behavioral health services. It adds and cuts money for substance abuse treatment, mental health services, and state psychiatric hospitals for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, and it adds 15 full-time jobs for Mental Health Services. It also lets two divisions move some money between pay and benefit costs, and it requires a report on Idaho Behavioral Health Plan spending by December 1, 2026. Sections 7 and 8 took effect on April 2, 2026, and the rest took effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1430.s: This law tightens Idaho’s rules on local firearm laws. It says counties, cities, and other local bodies generally cannot make or enforce their own rules on firearm sale, ownership, carrying, storage, and related items, and it sets a $10,000 civil penalty for willful violations. It also lets the attorney general, or a person or group harmed by a bad local rule, seek damages, court orders, or other relief after giving notice and time to fix the problem. It took effect on April 2, 2026.

ID-2026-S1433.s: This law changes funding for Idaho’s Department of Health and Welfare Medicaid division for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. It adds and removes money for Medicaid programs such as administration, coordinated, enhanced, basic, expansion, and hospital assessment funding. Sections for fiscal year 2025-2026 took effect on passage and approval, and the fiscal year 2026-2027 sections take effect July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1435.s: For fiscal year 2027, the bill would set funding for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and the State Independent Living Council. It covers many areas in the department, including child safety, early learning, welfare, Medicaid, and public health. The measure became law on April 2, 2026, as Chapter 271.

ID-2026-S1438.s: The law cuts $13.5 million from the Idaho Digital Learning Academy for fiscal year 2027 and reduces the related transfer from the state general fund by the same amount. It also bars withdrawals from the Public Education Stabilization Fund for the academy during that year and says the academy must use existing cash and may reduce offerings or turn away eligible enrollments to keep a positive cash balance. The academy must also submit reports on course compliance with state rules on diversity, equity, inclusion, and on its funding and course costs. It became law and takes effect on July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1439.s: The law changes rules for the Model School Facility Council, a group that studies school building plans and makes a model plan for schools to use. It moves the deadline for the council to send its plan to the Legislature from July 1, 2026, to July 1, 2027. The act became law and took effect on April 10, 2026.

ID-2026-S1448.s: This law changes Idaho rules on material that is harmful to minors. It updates some key word definitions, changes rules for sharing or showing sexually explicit material to minors, and sets rules for schools and public libraries on access and reviews of such material. It also keeps misdemeanor penalties for some public displays and store-location limits tied to sexual material. The law takes effect July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-S1453.s: This law creates an Idaho rural health transformation fund and a nine-member committee to help oversee how the money is used for rural health care. It gives the Department of Health and Welfare $3,737,600 for fiscal year 2026 and $295,405,200 for fiscal year 2027, and adds 12 full-time positions in each year. It also asks for a report on efforts to advance certain practice rule changes for physician assistants and dental hygienists.

ID-2026-S1454.s: This law increases money for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare for early learning and development, youth safety and permanency, and family and community partnerships for fiscal year 2027. It also adds three full-time jobs in Early Learning and Development, requires a report on the Idaho Home Visiting Program by December 31, 2026, and allows certain money transfers within these programs. The law took effect on April 10, 2026, with most parts starting July 1, 2026.

ID-2026-SCR127.s: This concurrent resolution is a formal statement from the Legislature that urges Idaho citizens to reject any effort to put the Idaho Medical Cannabis Act on the ballot. It says the proposal could set up a statewide marijuana program, including production, sales, online ordering, and home delivery, and it estimates $1.1 million in yearly costs plus $2.9 million in startup costs for one state agency. The resolution was delivered to the Secretary of State on April 2, 2026.

ID-2026-SCR128.s: The resolution would approve most temporary and pending state agency rules reviewed during the 2026 legislative session, but it would reject several listed parts and full dockets. It affects agencies including Agriculture, Health and Welfare, Fish and Game, Environmental Quality, Transportation, and others. Most approved pending rules would take effect on July 1, 2026, while a few listed dockets would take effect when the session ends.
